quote: Bewegt sich etwa das Elektron nach einem Minimumsatz und wie ist der Zusammenhang mit dem Helmholtz-Schwarzschild'schen Minimumsprincip?
english: Does the electron perhaps move according to a minimum theorem, and what is the connection with the Helmholtz–Schwarzschild minimum principle?
topic: The page notes Nernst's diffusion problem with a closed-form solution, a question about two Newtonian mass points colliding along a line, questions about minimum principles in optics and Maxwell's electrodynamics, and the start of a remark on Poincaré's idea of periodic cycles on Riemann surfaces.

triage.modern_statement: Can the equation of motion of a charged particle (the electron) in an electromagnetic field be derived from a variational (least-action) principle? And how does that principle relate to the Helmholtz–Schwarzschild action principle for electrodynamics, the 1903 Göttingen formulation in which one action integral gives both Maxwell's field equations and the forces on charges? In modern terms: write a single Lagrangian or action for fields plus charged particles, for example S = −Σ m c ∫ ds − Σ e ∫ A_μ dx^μ − (1/16πc) ∫ F_{μν}F^{μν} d^4x, or the field-free Schwarzschild–Tetrode–Fokker action for direct interaction between particles. Its Euler–Lagrange equations give the Lorentz-force motion of the electron.
triage.answered_by: Partly already answered when Hilbert wrote the note. Karl Schwarzschild (1903) had an action principle that covers point charges, and Schwarzschild found a force law between two point charges from it. It was developed further by Tetrode and by Fokker (1929; action for direct interaction between particles), then by Wheeler and Feynman (1949). Separately, Mie (1912–13) built a variational field theory of matter and the electron, which Born (1914) and Hilbert himself (Foundations of Physics, 1915) took up. Today the least-action derivation of charged-particle dynamics is textbook material. Questions about how to define a variational principle in the Wheeler–Feynman two-body setting were still being worked on in 2009 (De Luca).

evidence.claim: Wheeler and Feynman's 1949 review discusses the Schwarzschild–Tetrode–Fokker theory of direct interaction between particles and derives the motion of charged particles from Fokker's action principle. It also says Schwarzschild arrived at a force law between two point charges from his action.
A 2009 paper turns the formally defined Fokker action into a well-defined variational principle for the electromagnetic two-body problem.

Hilbert's 1915 Foundations of Physics drew closely on Mie's variational theory of matter and electrodynamics. Born showed in 1914 that Mie's variational principle could be recast in a particular form.
A review of least action in electrodynamics treats the action principle as the standard starting point for Lagrangian electrodynamics with charged particles.

triage.why: This is a real physics question: is there an action principle for electron motion, and how does it relate to Schwarzschild's 1903 electrodynamic action? It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. In its basic form it was settled, by Schwarzschild's own principle and later the Fokker and Wheeler–Feynman actions; the Lorentz-force motion now follows from a standard Lagrangian. Hilbert followed this line himself through Mie in 1915. Some refined versions are still being worked on: a 2009 paper on making the Wheeler–Feynman variational principle well-defined. A self-consistent variational treatment of an electron acting on itself (radiation reaction) was not checked in these searches. So I can't say how active the area is today. The searches did not turn up Helmholtz's own contribution, so how the note's 'Helmholtz–Schwarzschild' label maps onto specific papers is only partly confirmed.
